note.note:
History:
• Chief complaint: Progressive reduction in hearing in the left ear for ~6 weeks.  
• Course: Intermittent over the 6-week period.  
• Associated symptoms:  
  – Intermittent ringing (tinnitus) in the left ear.  
  – Occasional mild dizziness/off-balance; not true vertigo; no associated nausea.  
  – No ear pain, no otorrhea, no pruritus.  
• Triggers: Patient stated certain activities (watching TV, listening to music) “trigger” the tinnitus but also said they “solve” it – conflict noted.  
• Negatives: No fever, chest pain, palpitations.  
• Previous episode: Brief hearing difficulty ~1 year ago lasting only a couple of days.

Past Medical History:
• Chronic illnesses: Not documented.  
• Surgical / hospitalizations: Not documented.  
• Allergies: Not documented.  
• Medications: Not documented.  
• Preventive care / social history: Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
• Virtual visit – no direct examination performed.  
• Patient appears able to converse, suggesting no gross cognitive deficit.  
• Reported: No visible ear discharge.  
• No reported throat swelling, chest pain, or cardiac symptoms.

Impression:
Left-sided hearing loss with intermittent tinnitus and mild disequilibrium – rule out impacted cerumen vs middle/inner ear pathology.

Management Plan:
• Arrange face-to-face clinic visit within 4–5 days for otoscopic examination to assess for cerumen impaction or other structural causes.  
• Provide patient with tinnitus information leaflet (link placed in visit notes).  
• Patient instructed to call support team to book appointment; phone number added to chart.  
• Advised to avoid cotton buds/Q-tips.  
• Safety-net: If symptoms worsen (severe dizziness, pain, new discharge, hearing loss in right ear, chest pain, palpitations), schedule urgent video or in-person review.

Patient Summary:
Jack Smith (DOB 31 Oct 1990) reports 6 weeks of left-sided hearing decline with intermittent tinnitus and mild dizziness. Physical blockage such as impacted wax is suspected; an in-person otoscopic exam is planned to confirm and direct further care.

Key Takeaways:
1. Book in-person ear check within the next 4–5 days.  
2. Read the tinnitus leaflet to understand condition and limited treatment options.  
3. Seek urgent care if dizziness worsens or new symptoms develop.

Next Steps:
• Otoscopic examination; remove cerumen if present.  
• If ear canal clear, consider audiometry and evaluation for inner-ear or neurological causes.  
• Follow-up after examination to discuss findings and management.
